blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews David Parnas' 1971 paper on information distribution in system design, drawing parallels to modern microservices architecture. Parnas argues that inadvertent coupling between modules (or microservices) arises from uncontrolled information sharing, particularly internal implementation details. He emphasizes that exposing such details harms system modularity and maintainability, as programmers inevitably exploit available information, even when it leads to poor design decisions. Parnas advocates for strict control over information distribution, suggesting that only interface specifications (not internal details) should be shared. He also discusses the trade-offs in early system partitioning, noting that time pressures often lead to suboptimal modular boundaries. The paper highlights how early design decisions, especially those based on transient requirements, become harder to change as the system evolves. Parnas' key insight is that information control is critical to preserving system structure and enabling future modifications.
